name: Executive order of March 31, 1882 cutting the Havasupai (Suppai) reserve down to the floor of Cataract Canyon
citation: Executive order of March 31, 1882 (1 Kappler 809; Royce area 633)
nations: Havasupai Tribe (Havasuw 'Baaja, People of the Blue-Green Water)
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It revoked the order of November 23, 1880 and set apart in its place only the bottom land of the canyon of Cataract Creek between walls of red sandstone, from a stone monument about 2 miles above the village to the crest of the third falls (Royce p. 906; Kappler p. 809).
The Indian Claims Commission found the 1880 reserve it replaced was five miles wide and twelve long, about 38,400 acres, and that the 1882 order cut it to about 518.6 acres (finding 9).

breaches.what: The Commission found that this 1882 order took the Havasupai's Indian title to the roughly 38,400 acres of the 1880 reservation except the 518.6 acres it reserved, and that the tribe was never compensated; the June 8, 1880 order had already taken the land outside the reservation.

landTaken: The Commission found the 1882 order took the 1880 reservation of about 38,400 acres except 518.6 acres (finding 12). For the whole claim the parties determined 2,257,728 acres were appropriated without payment (additional findings, 1969).
compensation: $1,240,000 by stipulated final judgment of August 6, 1969 (Docket 91), a compromise.
today: The Grand Canyon National Park Enlargement Act of January 3, 1975 put about 185,000 acres into trust for the Havasupai as part of the reservation and gave the tribe use of about 95,300 acres of park land for grazing and traditional purposes (section 10). Interior said that since 1882 the tribe had been confined to 519 acres at the bottom of the canyon (press release, January 17, 1975).

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its home has been in and around the Grand Canyon along Havasu Creek since time immemorial, calls itself Guardians of the Grand Canyon and of its ancestral lands above and below the rims, and opposes uranium mining on those aboriginal lands.

openQuestions: Date: the Commission's findings, opinion and order all print the order as March 3, 1882, while Royce and the order itself (Kappler p. 809, via the American Presidency Project) date it March 31, 1882. Both cite 1 Kappler 809 and the same 518.6-acre reserve, so they are the same order; the Commission's date looks like a dropped digit. The interlocutory order also values the land as of "March 3, 1883".
The 1975 Act section 10(f) is recorded as an act-of-congress breach because it extinguished remaining Havasupai title by statute; it also returned land. Jordan may prefer it under today only.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. In 1880 a presidential order set apart about 38,400 acres in Cataract Canyon for the Havasupai; this 1882 order replaced it with about 518 acres of canyon floor.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found this order took the rest of the 1880 reservation without paying the Havasupai. Their whole claim was settled for $1,240,000 in 1969.
plain.today: In 1975 Congress put about 185,000 acres into trust for the tribe and allowed use of about 95,300 more acres of park land.
